The assistant, mobile experiences, free access and the question of what “open” means.
A clinical question usually comes with work attached. Once a clinician has checked whether a treatment fits the patient in front of them, there may be a note to write, a coverage request to prepare and a patient who needs to understand what happens next.
That follow-on work is what interests me most as a healthcare AI engineer. An assistant that helps with it has to produce an answer that still holds up after it leaves the chat window, when it has become a sentence in a chart or a paragraph in a letter to an insurer.
OpenEvidence is a good product to study with that in mind. It answers clinical questions with cited sources, and since August 2025 it has moved into the surrounding tasks: it can help draft a visit note and prepare paperwork intended to help a patient obtain treatment. Apple has also announced a research study, conducted with OpenEvidence, in which people can ask questions about their own health. OpenEvidence Visits, Access Intelligence, Apple’s announcement.
So I read the public record to understand what clinicians ask it, what the assistant does with an answer, who can use it for free and how much of it anyone can inspect. I worked from product documents, platform terms and published studies, without hands-on testing. Where I explain the product’s appeal, I am offering an interpretation of those sources.
What clinicians are asking OpenEvidence
A JAMA study examined the platform’s activity from January 2024 through June 2026. Over that period, 952,008 clinicians, including 556,200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries. That is a cumulative count across two and a half years. For a single month, June 2026, the study reported 703,265 monthly active users. The author group included OpenEvidence-affiliated researchers. JAMA study.
Those counts show use at scale. I learned more from what the study says about the kind of question. The researchers used a large language model (LLM) to classify a stratified sample of 38.8 million queries. Treatment and management accounted for 33.1% of that sample, and diagnosis for 13.9%.
 
Two query categories are shown, not an exhaustive breakdown. Source: the JAMA study’s 38.8-million-query sample. Classification was performed by an LLM. Queries are not patients or demonstrated improvements in care.
Diagnostic puzzles dominate many medical-AI demonstrations. This sample describes something more ordinary: substantial use around managing care.
The logs record what was asked and how it was categorized. They cannot tell us why a clinician chose the tool, how often the answers were correct or whether patients benefited. My own reading is that a clinician may already know the diagnosis and still need to resolve a question about the evidence, an exception or whether a treatment applies to this patient. Lowering the effort of investigating that question seems a plausible reason to come back.
The current product also lets a clinician decide how much time to spend on an answer. In its September 2026 release, OpenEvidence described Osler as its fast default, Sackett as a deeper and more interactive search model, and Snow as a longer investigation that produces a structured report. The company gives approximate response times of five seconds, thirty seconds and five minutes, respectively. Model-family announcement.
I like what that choice acknowledges. A question that comes up during a consultation may need a different response from one a clinician can investigate after clinic. Whether each mode meets that need still has to be evaluated.
A fourth model, Darwin, is an application-only research preview and sits outside the free product. Its reported results come up later, with the comparisons.
A small 2025 primary-care study gives one view of how an answer might be used. Four physicians rated OpenEvidence’s responses to five retrospectively selected cases involving common chronic conditions. They rated relevance at 3.75 out of 4, while the mean rating for impact on clinical decision-making was 1.95. The answers largely reinforced existing plans. That suggests a role as an evidence check, although five retrospective cases cannot establish a general benefit. Hurt and colleagues.
If the product’s first job is helping a clinician confirm or question a plan, the next thing to understand is what happens to the answer afterward.
What the assistant does after the answer
OpenEvidence launched Visits in August 2025. Its announcement describes encounter transcription, configurable note templates, evidence incorporated into assessment and plan drafting, and follow-up questions that use patient and visit context. It also describes uploading and querying patient documentation. As described, these capabilities place the assistant inside documentation work. Time saved and patient benefit are separate questions that need measurement. Visits announcement.
Consider a deliberately simplified workflow. A clinician asks a question, receives an evidence summary, then incorporates part of it into a note. Reviewing the final note means separating three things: what the patient reported, what the clinician observed and what the system proposed from the literature. A plausible recommendation should not become, by default, a fact about what happened in the encounter.
That is an engineering boundary I would want preserved in any interface of this kind. Source evidence and encounter evidence need distinct identities even when they appear in the same paragraph. This is my design requirement; I have not observed how OpenEvidence handles it.
Access Intelligence, announced November 11, 2026, moves into the work that follows a decision. OpenEvidence says it covers more than 2,500 patient-support programs, with information updated daily, and supports savings offers, enrollment materials and prior-authorization documents. Prior authorization is the process of seeking a payer’s approval before it will cover certain care. Access Intelligence announcement.
The company also says clinicians had already written more than 500,000 prior-authorization documents on the platform. That figure counts generated paperwork. It cannot tell us how many requests were approved, how many patients obtained treatment or whether staff spent less time correcting submissions.
Those are the measures I would use to judge this stage of the product. For an appeal letter, I want to know whether the factual account matches the chart, whether the cited policy applies and whether the letter addresses the payer’s stated reason for denial. A polished letter is one part of that work.
The product idea is persuasive: keep the evidence close to the tasks that depend on it. It also raises the cost of a mistake. An error in an answer can be caught while reading. An error carried into several downstream documents takes more work to locate and correct.
Features like these raise two practical questions. Who can use them, and how much of the system can anyone outside the company inspect?
Who gets free access, and which parts are open source
OpenEvidence’s headline offer is free access for verified U.S. healthcare professionals. Its model guide says Osler, Sackett and Snow are available to verified clinicians with unlimited usage at no cost. The clinical service is not free to every person who visits the website. OpenEvidence, model guide.
Free access is one property. Visible citations are another: an answer shows its sources, so a reader can follow a claim back to the literature.
Open-source software is a different property again. It gives a user rights to inspect, modify and redistribute code under its license. Public model weights would make trained model parameters available, subject to their own terms. Even a downloadable model would need its surrounding software, data access and operating infrastructure to reproduce a complete clinical service.
Is OpenEvidence open source? Parts of its tooling are public; the clinical system, as far as I could find, is not. Its GitHub organization lists projects such as a Celery health-check utility and repositories for common software libraries. That is useful public code, separate from the clinical answer engine. Its Hugging Face organization showed no public models when I checked for this article. GitHub organization, Celery utility, model listing.
The product’s terms grant a limited license to use the service. Its acceptable-use policy prohibits attempts to discover the underlying source code or algorithms through reverse engineering. The public materials I reviewed did not provide the production model weights, a complete training pipeline or a license to run the clinical service independently. As of the research date, the clinical product is a proprietary hosted service, with some public software around it. Terms, section 3, acceptable-use policy.
 
These categories describe different permissions. The assessment reflects public materials available on November 16, 2026; it is not a numerical openness score.
Access to the evidence is one more category. OpenEvidence has agreements with publishers including NEJM, JAMA, Nature and Cochrane. Those agreements can make otherwise hard-to-reach material useful inside a clinical tool. They do not turn every underlying article into openly licensed material that anyone can redistribute or use to train another model. OpenEvidence’s content partnerships, content-use restrictions.
It is fair to ask how much this matters to someone in clinic. Clinicians need useful answers rather than model weights. A clinician should not need to read source code before finding a tool useful, a proprietary tool can be useful, and open source would not by itself establish that medical answers are safe.
The transparency that matters most for clinical use also does not depend on publishing patient records or a publisher’s archive. A system can disclose how it was evaluated, identify the version in use and show exactly which source supports a claim.
Two mobile experiences for two different audiences
Mobile is where access is easiest to misread, because two separate things are involved.
The first is OpenEvidence’s own clinician app. Its U.S. App Store listing identifies OpenEvidence Inc. as the developer, lists a zero download price and explicitly requires healthcare-professional verification. The listing dates its original release to August 2024. A free download does not change eligibility: the verification requirement applies on the phone too. Official App Store listing.
The second is much newer and belongs to Apple. On November 15, 2026, Apple announced the Apple Health AI Usage Study, conducted with OpenEvidence. It is a U.S. research study with an associated app, intended to examine trust, comprehension, answer quality and people’s engagement with conversational health AI. Participants can ask health questions and see citations. They can also choose to share certain HealthKit data, such as sleep, activity, resting heart rate or lab results. Apple’s study announcement.
 
Shared medical sources do not give clinicians and patients the same context for interpreting an answer. Illustration, not a screenshot of either app.
The announced capacity is up to 200,000 eligible participants, which is a recruitment ceiling and should not be read as an enrollment count. Participants must be at least 21, live in the United States and have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone running iOS 26 or later. Apple also says study data will not be used to train AI models and that sharing HealthKit data and survey responses is under participants’ control.
The change in audience is what makes the research necessary. A clinician may read an answer with a diagnosis, medication list and physical examination in mind. A patient may be trying to work out whether a symptom deserves attention, or what a lab result means. The same reference can be interpreted very differently in those two settings.
For a consumer experience, I would look past whether an answer sounds understandable. I would want to know whether the person understands its uncertainty, whether it helps them prepare a better question for their clinician, and whether it could create false reassurance or unnecessary alarm. Those are my proposed evaluation questions. Apple has announced a study design, so better preparation for a clinical conversation is a possibility the study can test.
How to check a citation before the claim travels
Both audiences are shown citations, and that is one of the most useful things about the product. A visible source gives the reader somewhere to go next.
It also creates a tempting shortcut. A real paper beneath a fluent answer can make the answer feel verified before anyone has checked whether the paper supports it.
A July 2026 pharmacy critique in JACCP supplies a concrete example. The authors examined responses to a question about incomplete miscarriage, including queries made in May and November 2025. They reported that the system relied on studies whose populations excluded the condition asked about. In the later response, it also made conflicting claims using the same source and assigned an efficacy figure to the wrong intervention. Bergsbaken and colleagues, full article.
The critique is illustrative and based on 2025 queries, so it says nothing about the product’s current error rate. Its lasting value is the mechanism it shows. A reference can exist, concern the right broad topic and still fail to support the sentence attached to it. The population, comparison and outcome have to match the question too.
 
An author-designed review process. It does not depict OpenEvidence’s internal architecture.
The two aids below offer a way to make that check routine. Both are my own proposals for manual review. They are not product features, I have not tested them inside OpenEvidence, and they have not been validated to reduce errors.
The first is a follow-up prompt a clinician could adapt after an initial question:

A better-shaped answer can still be wrong, so the next step is to open the consequential source and compare it with the claim. In the published miscarriage example, checking the study’s excluded population would have exposed the mismatch.
The second aid is for a claim that needs to be retained. A compact review record preserves more context than a screenshot of the answer alone:
Question and date: What was asked, and when
Product mode or visible version: Which system produced the answer
Decision-relevant claim: The exact statement being considered
Source and location: The article, guideline section or table
Applicability: Why its population and comparison fit, or do not fit
Reviewer’s conclusion: Supported, unsupported or still unresolved
Intended use: Whether the claim is informational or will enter a note, letter or decision
The record captures the reasoning a future reviewer would need. No model weights are required to notice that a paper excludes the population in the question.
What comparative studies say, and which versions they describe
Checking one claim at a time is slow, so it is natural to want a shortcut: which tool is simply more accurate? The published comparisons help, within their dates.
A Nature Medicine study compared OpenEvidence and UpToDate Expert AI with GPT-5.2, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview and Claude Opus 4.6. It included 500 MedQA questions, 500 HealthBench items and 100 de-identified questions collected from clinicians using an LLM in practice. Twelve clinicians performed randomized, blinded reviews of answers to the clinical questions. The general-purpose models performed better on the study’s evaluations. Vishwanath and colleagues.
That result is a reason for caution about choosing a clinical tool on specialist branding alone. Its limits matter just as much. The study accessed OpenEvidence in September 2025 and February 2026, so it cannot settle how the September 2026 model family performs. The researchers did not evaluate citation quality or response latency, and the clinical questions originated in use of a general-purpose model. One author disclosed consulting for Google, among other interests.
OpenEvidence subsequently reported a perfect MedQA score for Darwin and other strong benchmark results. Those are company-reported results for a restricted research model, and they should not be attributed to every answer from Osler, Sackett or Snow. The two sets of results concern different systems, times and evaluation conditions, so neither cancels the other. Darwin announcement.
The question for a clinician today is narrower than any ranking: how does the available version, in the intended workflow, perform on the kinds of questions they need answered?
Teams that want to answer it systematically should arrange authorized access first. OpenEvidence’s acceptable-use policy restricts automated collection and certain systematic querying without authorization, and its research-preview route is distinct from an unrestricted public API. Acceptable-use policy, research-access description.
How free access is paid for, and how the data policies differ
Unlimited use at no cost has to be funded somehow. Advertising helps support OpenEvidence’s free service. Its advertising policies require ads to be identifiable and set rules intended to keep advertising distinct from clinical content. The JACCP critique also discusses advertising as the business model supporting free access. Advertising policies, JACCP critique.
The arrangement lowers the subscription barrier for clinicians, which I count as valuable. It also makes the separation between commercial interests and medical answers consequential. I found policy commitments and no evidence that an advertiser had influenced a particular answer; the existence of ads is no basis for inferring it. A policy is also different from an independent audit.
What a reader or researcher can observe is concrete: whether sponsored placements are unmistakable, whether they can be told apart from evidence, whether alternative treatments and conflicting findings are represented appropriately, and whether researchers can study those questions under a clear access arrangement.
Data use deserves the same precision. OpenEvidence’s privacy policy states that it does not train AI models on protected health information. It separately discusses professional account data, advertising and some research and development uses of aggregated or de-identified information. Each statement has its own scope, and the policy supports neither “it never uses data” nor a claim that it trains on patient records. Privacy policy.
For a healthcare organization, the relevant question is how a specific feature handles the information its staff will submit, under the applicable agreement and local rules. The clinical app’s policy and Apple’s study commitments should be reviewed separately, because they cover different services and different participants.
What I’ll be watching, and one habit to keep
I began with the work attached to a clinical question. OpenEvidence’s appeal, as I read the public record, is that it lowers the effort and subscription cost of reaching medical knowledge, then puts that knowledge beside the note and the paperwork that follow.
The evidence I would most like to see is tied to that same work. Independent evaluations of the current named models would help, since published results apply to specific versions and dates. So would prospective studies of what happens in practice: fewer unsupported claims in final notes, less correction time for clinicians, coverage requests that address the right criteria, and patients who understand their next steps more accurately. Those outcomes would tell me more than another count of generated answers. Results from Apple’s study, when they come, should say something about how people outside the clinic read a cited answer.
The habit is available today, and it needs nothing from the company. When an answer is about to become a note, an appeal or a clinical decision, open the source behind the sentence. Check that its population, comparison and outcome match the question, and that you can explain why it supports the words you are about to use.
Research note: This article reviews public product documents, platform terms, an App Store record and published studies as of November 16, 2026. It is not a hands-on clinical validation of OpenEvidence. Product claims, study findings and my proposed design or review practices are identified separately. Illustrations were created in Midjourney; diagrams and charts were created in Excalidraw using Geist Serif.

For a one-person software factory, the question is not how many models you connect. It is whether they complete real work reliably and affordably.

Last night I set up an AI on my MacBook that doesn't refuse anything. No account, no API key, no internet needed, and not one byte of my chats leaving the laptop.
Setup took about 15 minutes, and most of that was waiting for a 7 GB download.
This is the guide I wish I'd had: what to install on a Mac or a Windows PC, which model fits your RAM, the settings that actually matter, and how to keep a copy of the weights for yourself.
It's long, so bookmark it.
For education and lawful personal use only. "Uncensored" means the model stops lecturing and refusing. It doesn't make anything legal that wasn't legal before. What you do with it is on you.
Why now
Hugging Face recently disabled an abliterated GLM-5.3 build. Journalists counted more than 6,500 "uncensored" models on the site and asked why the rest are still up.
I don't know where this ends. I do know a model on your own disk can't be taken down, can't be quietly "updated" and doesn't send your prompts to anyone.
That's the whole point of this article.
What "uncensored" means (and what it doesn't)
 
Chat models learn a "refusal direction" during safety training. Hit it and you get "I'm sorry, I can't help with that", even for a chemistry exam question or a dark scene in a novel.
You'll see three kinds of uncensored model:
Abliterated. Someone finds that refusal direction and subtracts it from the weights. No retraining. The model is otherwise the same.
Heretic. Abliteration done by an automated tool that hunts for the fewest refusals with the smallest change to the model. Good uploads publish their numbers, like "refusals 99/100 → 0/100, KL divergence 0.03". A low KL means almost nothing else changed.
Fine-tuned. Retrained on data without refusals (Dolphin is the famous one). It gets a different personality, which you might like more or less.
Two things people get wrong:
It isn't smarter. A 12B model is still a 12B model, just without the reflex to say no.
It still makes things up, now with zero hedging. Check anything that matters.
Step 1: check how much memory you have
 
The only spec that really matters is memory.
Mac (M1 to M5): the GPU shares RAM with everything else ("unified memory"), and macOS gives it roughly two-thirds to three-quarters. A 16 GB MacBook has about 11 GB for a model.
Windows: what counts is your graphics card's VRAM. NVIDIA is the easy path; AMD works through Vulkan. If a model doesn't fit, it spills into normal RAM and gets a lot slower.
To check: on a Mac, Apple menu → About This Mac. On Windows, Ctrl+Shift+Esc → Performance → GPU → "Dedicated GPU memory".
My rule of thumb: the file size plus 20–30% has to fit. That extra is the memory the conversation itself uses.
Quantization, briefly
 
Models are shipped compressed ("quantized") in a format called GGUF. Every repo offers several versions:
Q4_K_M is the one to download. About a quarter of the original size, and you won't notice the difference in chat.
Q5/Q6 if you have memory to spare.
Q8 is basically lossless but twice the size.
Q3/IQ3 squeezes a bigger model onto a smaller machine, with a noticeable drop in quality.
A bigger model at Q4 almost always beats a smaller one at Q8.
Step 2: pick a model
 
These are the ones I'd actually download in November 2026. Sizes are Q4_K_M unless I say otherwise. The name after each one is the Hugging Face repo, so you can paste it straight into a search.
8 GB (any recent laptop)
Gemma 4 E4B Abliterated, 5.3 GB. Small, quick, understands images.
mradermacher/Huihui-gemma-4-E4B-it-abliterated-GGUF
Ornith 1.5 9B Uncensored, 5.6 GB. Surprisingly good at code for its size.
mradermacher/Ornith-1.5-9B-uncensored-GGUF
16 GB (MacBook Air/Pro 16 GB, RTX 3060 12 GB, 4060 Ti)
Gemma 4 12B Heretic, 7.4 GB. If you only download one model, make it this one. It's the one in my screenshots and the demo video.
igorls/gemma-4-12B-it-heretic-GGUF
Qwen3.5 9B Defiant Fable Heretic, 7.0 GB. Over 2 million downloads in the last month.
DavidAU/Qwen3.5-9B-The-Defiant-Fable-Uncensored-Heretic-NEO-IMATRIX-MAX-MTP-GGUF
GPT-OSS 20B Heretic, 11.8 GB (IQ4_NL). OpenAI's open model without the refusals. Fast because only part of it runs per token.
DavidAU/OpenAi-GPT-oss-20b-HERETIC-uncensored-NEO-Imatrix-gguf
24–32 GB (MacBook Pro 24–36 GB, RTX 3090/4090/5090)
Qwen3.8 27B Abliterated, 16.8 GB. The most downloaded uncensored model on Hugging Face right now (about 4.2M a month), and the smartest thing in this tier. On a 16 GB card, use the 11.8 GB GSQ-IQ3_S file.
huihui-ai/Huihui-Qwen3.8-27B-abliterated-GGUF
Gemma 4 31B Abliterated, 18.7 GB. Best writer of the bunch.
mradermacher/gemma-4-31B-it-abliterated-GGUF
Gemma 4 26B-A4B Abliterated, 16.8 GB. Only 4B parameters active per token, so it stays fast even when it doesn't fully fit.
mradermacher/Huihui-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-abliterated-GGUF
Dolphin Mistral 24B Venice, 14.3 GB. The old favourite for fiction and roleplay.
bartowski/cognitivecomputations_Dolphin-Mistral-24B-Venice-Edition-GGUF
LFM2.5 24B-A2B Uncensored, 15.4 GB. 2B active parameters, very fast, built for agents.
AtomicChat/LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Uncensored-GGUF
64–128 GB (Mac Studio, MacBook Pro Max, multi-GPU)
GPT-OSS 120B Heretic v2, 63 GB (MXFP4).
bartowski/kldzj_gpt-oss-120b-heretic-v2-GGUF
Qwen3.8 Flash-Next Abliterated, 68 GB (IQ2_XS). 125B parameters, 6B active.
SC117/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-abliterated-GGUF
 
Step 3: install LM Studio and chat (Mac)
This is the no-terminal route, and it's what I used. LM Studio is free, and after the download it works with no internet at all.
1. Download it from lmstudio.ai and drag it into Applications.
Heads up: I first put the app on my external SSD to save space. It launched, showed no window and just sat there. It only runs from /Applications. Your models can live anywhere, though (more on that below).
2. Open it and skip the starter-model suggestion.
3. Click Model Search in the left sidebar and type gemma-4-12B-it-heretic.
4. Pick igorls/gemma-4-12B-it-heretic-GGUF, choose the Q4_K_M file and download it. Read the model card while you wait. This one even tells you to keep "thinking" off for the most reliable answers.
 
5. Click Use in New Chat. The model loads and you're chatting.
6. Optional: in Library, select the model and open the Load tab. I keep GPU offload at max and context at 8K, and raise the context only when I'm pasting long documents.
 
7. Ask it something. Speed shows under every answer. On my M4 Pro it does about 28 tokens per second, which is faster than I read.
 
Keeping models on an external drive: in Library, the models folder is shown in the bottom-right corner. Point it at your SSD. All my models live on an external drive, and loading speed is fine.
Same thing on Windows
1. Update your GPU driver first. Most "why is it so slow" problems are an old driver.
2. Download LM Studio for Windows from lmstudio.ai and install it.
3. Model Search → find the model → Q4_K_M → download → Use in New Chat.
4. In the load settings, push GPU Offload up until it stops fitting. If a model is too big, LM Studio splits it between the GPU and RAM by itself.
5. Under Settings → Runtime, pick CUDA for NVIDIA or Vulkan for AMD and Intel.
If you live in the terminal: Ollama
 
Ollama runs models as a local server, which is what you want if you're wiring a model into scripts, agents or a web UI.
Install it from ollama.com (Ollama.dmg on Mac, OllamaSetup.exe on Windows). Then one command pulls any GGUF straight from Hugging Face and starts a chat:
 
The commands I actually use:
 
Turn thinking off for Gemma 4 and Qwen3.x uncensored builds. The refusal removal targets the normal answer mode. With thinking on, refusals creep back and long reasoning can eat the whole reply. Use /set nothink in chat, or send "think": false through the API.
To keep Ollama's models on another drive, set OLLAMA_MODELS to a folder there and restart Ollama. On a Mac: launchctl setenv OLLAMA_MODELS /Volumes/YourDrive/ollama. On Windows, add it under System → Environment Variables.
Want a ChatGPT-style window on top? Open WebUI connects to Ollama at http://localhost:11434.
Settings worth touching
 
System prompt. Abliterated models still have assistant habits. I use: "You are a direct assistant. Answer fully and factually. Skip disclaimers."
Temperature. 0.7 for chat and writing, 0.3 for code and facts.
Context. 8K is plenty for chat. Every step up costs memory.
GPU offload (Windows). As many layers on the GPU as fit. Even a few on the CPU slow everything down.
Thinking. Off for normal use. Turn it on for math and logic puzzles if the model supports it.
Back up the weights
 
You only keep what you've downloaded. A 1–2 TB external SSD is enough for a serious collection.
What I keep for every model I use:
the Q4_K_M GGUF (plus Q8 when there's room)
the original base model (for example Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B), because uncensored versions come and go
the model card and license
the LM Studio and Ollama installers, since apps disappear too
To download a whole repo or a single quant (Mac and Windows):
 
Check that the file isn't corrupted with shasum -a 256 model.gguf on a Mac or certutil -hashfile model.gguf SHA256 on Windows, and compare the result with the hash on the file's Hugging Face page.
If you have the space, also grab the big ones you can't run yet: Qwen3.8 Flash-Next, GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. Hardware gets cheaper; download links don't always last.
Don't get burned
 
Only download .gguf or .safetensors. Old .bin, .pt and .pkl files can run code when loaded.
Stick to known uploaders (bartowski, mradermacher, unsloth, huihui-ai, lmstudio-community) and look at downloads and likes before you click.
A real model is a data file. If something comes with an .exe or an "installer", close the tab.
After downloading you can go fully offline. Everything keeps working.
When something breaks
Crashes on load or "model too large": use a smaller quant, a smaller model or a shorter context.
1–3 tokens per second: the model is spilling out of GPU memory. Go smaller, or pick one with few active parameters (Gemma 26B-A4B, LFM2.5, GPT-OSS).
It still refuses now and then: thinking off, add the system prompt, regenerate. No uncensored build removes 100% of refusals.
Gibberish: update LM Studio or Ollama. New model families need new versions.
Fans spinning up on a Mac: normal. It's doing real work.
The short version
1. Check your memory.
2. Install LM Studio (or Ollama).
3. Download Gemma 4 12B Heretic with 16 GB, or Qwen3.8 27B Abliterated with 32 GB.
4. Thinking off, short system prompt, chat.
5. Copy the GGUF to an external drive today.
If this saved you an evening of googling, a bookmark or a repost helps it reach more people. Next I'll write up how I plug a local model into coding agents. Follow @0xProbabillity if you want that one.

Good morning. Nvidia's chief executive resigned. Anthropic and Google both published new model prices.
1. Fireworks AI breach reached customers, Notion and Cursor say (3 min read)
Fireworks AI says a breach it first disclosed October 9 reached its development machines on October 24 and touched account and billing details and, for some customers, stored keys, datasets and incomplete models. Notion says the breach exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in under 1% of workspaces, some with API keys, the passwords software uses to log in to services, pasted inside. Cursor says its Fireworks key exposed old coding-agent logs from sessions with Privacy Mode off, which led to the fake extension it pulled on October 29; at most 5,000 users may have received it.
→ These customers chose Notion and Cursor, which sent their data on to Fireworks. I'd ask every software vendor with an AI feature to name the outside companies that run its AI models and how long each keeps my data, and I'd have anyone who pasted a password into an AI chat change it.
 
2. United bars customers' unauthorized AI agents from booking
United says that since November 11, customers' AI agents may not search, book, buy or manage travel on its website or app, or through travel agencies, without its permission. United says an agent holding a customer's login can book or spend miles the customer never approved, and automated check-in can break federal rules that need a person to confirm the bags hold no banned items.
→ Customers are starting to send AI agents to do business on company websites. I'd decide whether my own site blocks them, lets them look but not buy, or lets them act after the customer signs in, and put that in the terms of use.
 
3. Claude Fable 5.2 costs a fifth less than 5.1 (7 min read)
Anthropic, which makes the Claude models that draft this newsletter, released Fable 5.2 on November 9, including on the Amazon, Google and Microsoft clouds. It lists at $8 per million tokens (the chunks of text a model reads and writes) in and $40 out, against $10 and $50 for Fable 5.1, and Anthropic says it runs up to 30% faster. Customers without zero data retention, an arrangement where Anthropic keeps none of their prompts, have prompts kept 30 days for safety monitoring.
→ Fable 5.1's API rates are higher than 5.2's, and GitHub drops the older Fable 5 from Copilot, its coding assistant, on December 14 (item 4). I'd test 5.2 on that work and check whether its prompt retention terms fit my data rules before moving anything sensitive.
4. Gemini 4 Carbon's launch price ends November 30 (1 min read)
Google opened Gemini 4 Carbon, which it calls its strongest model, to paying developers on November 10. Google's price list for its API, the connection developers' software uses, has Carbon at $2 in and $10 out per million tokens until November 30, then $4 and $20. The cheaper Gemini 4 Hydrogen, out November 12, is $1.50 and $7.50. GitHub says it drops Argon, Claude Fable 5 and 4 other models from Copilot on December 14, and turns on Carbon, Hydrogen and Fable 5.2 for Business and Enterprise organizations on default settings.
→ A cost test run on Carbon this month uses a price that ends in 2 weeks. I'd price Carbon at $4 and $20, against $8 and $40 for Fable 5.2, check which Copilot models my organization has set by hand before December 14, and test whether Hydrogen is enough for routine work.
 
5. Jensen Huang resigns; Nvidia names an interim chief (3 min read)
Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive and director on November 11, effective immediately, according to its securities filing. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive while the board looks for a permanent one, and Harvey Jones, a director since 1993, became chair. The filing gives no reason, and Jones says the board expects customer commitments and the product roadmap to "continue without interruption."
→ Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday, November 17, and I'd read them for anything on chip supply. I wouldn't change an AI chip or cloud plan on this news alone, or let a vendor use it to rush me into a long computing contract.
6. CoreWeave expects $9 billion in customer prepayments (18 min read)
CoreWeave, which rents out computing power for AI, reported quarterly revenue of $3.7 billion and a $709 million loss on November 10. It counts about $132.5 billion in orders it has taken but not yet filled, some estimated, and its chief executive expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits in the next 3 months.
→ CoreWeave expects customers to help fund its expansion through prepayments. If a computing provider asked me to pay up front, I'd check whether it can deliver and negotiate delivery dates, refund rights and penalties before committing.
 
7. IBM and Microsoft launch Imagine Enterprise for AI agents (6 min read)
IBM and Microsoft launched Imagine Enterprise on November 10, a platform for building, running and governing AI agents that bundles what they call "more than 6,000 AI agents and assets" from IBM Consulting on Microsoft's Azure cloud. The announcement offers access through IBM Consulting but gives no price and no named customer in production. Its one named client, SEI, is exploring AI agents with IBM Consulting.

Which sites ran the same trials, and who has a stake in the answer?
TLDR: Too Long, Did Not Read Answer is Probably Not.
I will start this off with the fact that I am obviously biased, but at the same time I am on the record for discussing some of the benefits that  private equity is hopefully bringing to our industry. It is becoming clear to me that the private equity backed site networks want, no, NEED, more market share and the feasibility surveys are Exhibit A.  At Yuma Clinical Trials, an independent community-based site, the people who answer the feasibility survey are the people who screen and randomize the patients. On one study we read the eligibility criteria and figured we could enroll 20 to 25 in about six months. After the sponsor turned us down, they told me the plan was five sites at 60 patients apiece because that is what some site networks promised. I’d answered their question. I wish I’d asked how many sites they planned to open.
That was a foreshadowing. The chart I saw on LinkedIn this morning was about patients who actually finished trials. Completion is the culmination of patient retention, one of the things independent sites actually do well in my opinion. I guess we are at Exhibit B now. Tufts reported average completion of 80.2% at network-affiliated sites, 41.8% in its combined independent and part-time group, and 24.0% at academic medical centers.
 
This chart is impressive
 
I believe those are the averages they saw. We are now left to wonder (after being impressed by a multitude of random statistics) how much of the gap would survive if both teams ran the same study, head to head comparisons, using the same initial raw data? Here is the link to the study if you want to be bedazzled.
Read the Association of Multisite Research Corporations caption alongside the graphic. The bar says “Independent AND part-time.” The caption turns that into 42% “for independent sites” and asks what full integration might deliver “if network affiliation alone moves performance this far.” Translation: How much better things could be sponsor if you ONLY used private equity backed site networks! 
great caption!
Drop “and part-time” and you’ve given my dedicated research site as well as every other private community based independent site a performance record the authors never measured separately for reasons unbeknownst to any of us yet we are supposed to go along with it like it is Gospel.
Where the headline came from
Ten sponsors and CROs took part in this "study". The authors describe 857 sites across 15 studies, with some performance data from 693 sites. Table 10’s three site-type counts add up to 693. In Table 11, the three completion counts add up to 463. Completion means that a randomized patient finished the study. The article supplies no patient totals behind the site averages.
 
Table 10
 
Table 11
March/April report and definitions
How two groups can tie on each trial and finish 36 points apart
I give Tufts credit for getting sponsors and CROs to share operating data that site owners rarely get to see. Each contributor supplied site- and protocol-level information from one to three studies. The authors call the small sponsor sample their main limitation. They never say how they selected the protocols or how many had completion data from both groups. That overlap matters. I’d like to see head-to-head completion rates within each trial where both groups supplied data. If there were too few such trials, say so. That would have been an easier and more fair comparison although I suspect those results did not generate the headline numbers they were going for, but that is purely speculation on my part.
Here is why that head-to-head comparison matters. Imagine two protocols with ten randomized patients at every site. On Protocol A, lets say a 2 visit vaccine study that is relatively simple,  nine out of ten patients finish at every location. On Protocol B, lets say a 96 week heart failure trial that is far more complex, three out of ten finish at every location.
Protocol A · 90% finish at every site: Network sites: 8 sites; Unaffiliated sites: 2 sites.
Protocol B · 30% finish at every site: Network sites: 2 sites; Unaffiliated sites: 8 sites.
Total patients who finish: Network sites: 78 of 100; Unaffiliated sites: 42 of 100.
Where did the 36-point lead come from? Network sites enrolled 80 of their 100 patients in the trial that was easier to finish. Independent sites enrolled 80 of theirs in the harder trial. On the vaccine study, both groups finished at 90%. On the heart failure trial, both finished at 30%. The entire gap came from which trials the sites ran.
I made up these numbers. They illustrate the mistake Darrell Huff describes in “Post Hoc Rides Again,” a chapter in How to Lie with Statistics. Give network affiliation credit for those 36 points and you’ve credited it with an advantage that does not exist if you were to  compare sites on the same trial (which still has me scratching my head as to why that was not done).
That’s what I wanted Tufts to publish. On the same protocols where dedicated independent sites and network sites both enrolled patients, how many did each group randomize, and how many finished? The network advantage might still hold up, who knows? Anecdotally I think they would both have similar completers across the board for what it's worth, but I'm just a Youtuber and site owner, not a think tank. Unfortunately, the published study does not answer that question even though I think it could/should.
The concern has a clinical basis. In a separate Tufts study, phase II and III oncology protocols averaged 31.4% completion versus 80.0% for non-oncology. That benchmark used patients enrolled as its denominator. In the landscape survey, 61.0% of network respondents reported vaccine work, compared with 15.3% of academic respondents. The oncology difference was much smaller. It was 29.9% in networks and 35.1% at academic centers. Those were survey respondents. Table 11 I posted above separately says 16% of network sites were in vaccine trials. It never gives the vaccine share of the 23 sites reporting completion. Protocol mix is a credible explanation whose contribution we can’t quantify, and it may also be a reason for why they made this analysis so complex in trying to answer two questions as opposed to the headline grabbing one.
Tufts never tells us how many of the 23 network sites reporting completion were running vaccine trials. That matters because the mix of protocols could explain some or all of the gap. To answer the question raised by the headline, we didn’t need Claude. Sponsors and CROs had already supplied site- and protocol-level performance data. What I wanted to see was how many patients finished at each type of site on the same trial. If too few trials had completion data from both groups, say so. Claude came in because Tufts also wanted to answer a different question about how much trial activity each type of site accounts for. It helped build a list of networks and academic centers so the researchers could classify FDA investigator records. That may help estimate where the work goes. It still leaves a reader wondering whether a network site would retain more patients on the particular trial it’s trying to place.
What the statistical test can answer
Tufts reports a p-value below 0.001 for completion across all three site groups. That tells us there’s evidence that at least one group’s average differed from the others. The specific head-to-head result the authors highlight is for screen failure. On completion, they never tell us how large the gap was between network and unaffiliated sites running the same protocol, or give a confidence interval for that gap.
That distinction matters. Sites on the same trial follow the same eligibility criteria and visit schedule. Several of the 23 network sites could also belong to one company and share staff or systems. The article doesn’t say how many owners those sites represent or how the analysis accounted for those ties. Even on the same protocol, sponsors choose which sites participate, and those sites may draw patients from different referral sources. Patients were randomized to treatment. Nobody randomly assigned the clinics to join a network.
My bet is that dedicated independent sites and network sites would have similar completion rates head to head. I’d challenge the authors to show us how many patients each group randomized and how many finished on the protocols they had in common. If the network advantage holds up, I want to know by how much. And since sponsors also care about enrollment, I’d ask one separate question: what percentage of sites in each group actually met the enrollment target they agreed to?
Which patients and sites counted
Darrell Huff describes a neighborhood with a mean family income of $15,000 and a median of $3,500. In my two-clinic example, one finishes 2 of 2 patients and the other finishes 4 of 8. The mean and median site rates are both 75%. Across patients, 6 of 10 finished, or 60%. Now let me pick which clinic to call the network after I see the scores. I can make either group win. In a real study, somebody else ought to be able to check how each clinic got its label.
Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics, illustrated by Irving Geis (W. W. Norton, 1954), chapters 2, 7, 8 and 10. Book and chapter list
Who counts as an independent site
On the same protocol, say a full-time network site and a full-time independent each finish 8 of 10 patients. An unaffiliated part-time practice finishes 4 of 10. The dedicated sites tied, yet the published grouping would give networks an 80% to 60% lead. If all ten at the part-time practice finish, the combined group wins 90% to 80%. Tufts gives us no separate rate for dedicated independents and one has to wonder why.
The March/April report found the same ordering, with 70.6%, 31.3% and 21.5% for networks, the combined group and academic centers respectively. Its performance table covered 12 phase II/III studies and 524 sites. The authors, survey dates and response count line up with October. The reports don’t reconcile which performance records overlap. I take the consistency seriously, but I would want an independently assembled sample before treating it as replication and I would hope study sponsors are just as discerning.
How 1,154 replies became a market-share estimate
I understand why Tufts went beyond the sponsor data. Fifteen selected protocols can tell you something about those studies. They give you no reliable way to count how much work each kind of site does worldwide. For that question the researchers used a site survey and FDA investigator records. Sponsors supplied the patient completion figures separately. The issue I have is that the market-share analysis does not establish that site networks retain more patients. That question needs a comparison of completion rates within the same trials.
The survey got 1,154 replies from people. To estimate how many physical sites they represented, Tufts looked for matches on geography, ownership, network status, first study year and rare-disease work. It allowed annual volumes to differ by up to ten trials and required at least 80% overlap in the listed therapeutic areas and phases. Two coordinators at Yuma Clinical Trials could remember our first study year differently and get counted separately. Two sister network clinics with similar answers could get combined. The article reports no check against known site identities.
The matching exercise produced an estimate of 1,090 sites. Look at the next table.
 
Table 2
Its three counts are 555, 522 and 77. They add to 1,154, and 77 divided by 1,154 gives the published 6.7%. Where did the 64 extra replies fall? If a network and an unaffiliated practice each did one survey per location, but several people at one university answered, the university would get extra weight. The reverse is possible. Tufts gives no count of distinct sites by segment, response rate or check against the population of eligible sites. Even perfect matching would leave the question of who chose to respond.
Here is the multiplication behind Table 2. Weight each group’s replies by its average number of principal investigators (PIs) per site and by the FDA-derived activity per PI over five years. The last column is each group’s result divided by the total across all three.
Academic medical center: Replies: 555; PIs/site × activity/PI: 8.26 × 2.31; Share: 53.8%.
Independent and part-time: Replies: 522; PIs/site × activity/PI: 4.67 × 2.89; Share: 35.8%.
Network-affiliated: Replies: 77; PIs/site × activity/PI: 5.67 × 4.68; Share: 10.4%.
For networks, 77 × 5.67 × 4.68 gives roughly 2,043 units of estimated activity. The three groups total about 19,678. Divide 2,043 by 19,678 and you get 10.4%. I can reproduce all three percentages from the printed inputs. Networks come out above their share of replies because their modeled activity per site is higher. That advantage is already in the inputs.
Again, the point of all of this was never to address the headline question of which site type has a higher patient completion rate. A within-trial comparison wherever both groups supplied completion data would give us a better clue. We don’t know how many of the 15 trials would qualify. Sometimes more data raises more questions than it purportedly answers, and this seems to be a chronic condition of the clinical research industry as a whole.
Tufts used Claude to help generate a list of network and academic names for matching FDA records. People reviewed the list and used text rules such as “University” to label records. If a network buys a clinic that keeps its local name, the match can miss it. Assigning a clinic’s earlier filings to its current owner could also credit a buyer for work done before the sale. Tufts gives no validation against dated affiliations. The survey matching and the sponsor completion analysis are separate from this AI step.
The authors and their financial relationships
Darrell Huff asks “Who says so?” I’m a site owner with a YouTube channel dedicated to smaller sites, I've already admitted my bias but I think we should have a fair comparison. I see the feasibility surveys that reach Yuma, and my business has money riding on the answers. When a sponsor passes on us, I rarely get to see how the winning site did, although occasionally we get asked to come on as a rescue site because I guess other sites didn't fulfill their promises, but I digress. I’d like the same candor from the people behind this research. The clearest author-level relationship I could document was Kenneth Getz’s board appointment at WCG, a company that offers network affiliation to independent sites amongst a slew of other services including centralized IRB offerings.
Kenneth Getz
Getz directs Tufts CSDD. WCG announced his appointment to its board of directors in December 2023, and WCG’s 2025 conference biography still identified him as a board member in the year the survey was fielded. WCG offers independent sites nonexclusive network affiliation and markets its network to sponsors. Private equity firm Arsenal Capital Partners lists WCG in its healthcare portfolio. Sponsors’ willingness to route studies through networks matters to a company selling that service. The October guest column mentions Getz’s board appointments generally. I could not verify his board status on publication day, his compensation or equity, or whether WCG contributed funds or data to this project.
Joan Chambers and Abigail Dirks
Chambers is a senior consultant advising research and membership programs. Tufts names her as the contact for its Circle of Supporters. Annual sponsors may discuss findings with faculty, help identify research priorities and receive member rates on working-group studies. Earlier in her career, Chambers was VP of marketing and strategy at Clin-X, whose affiliated businesses included ClinEdge and BTC Network. That history is relevant experience. It does not establish a continuing financial stake. Dirks is the center’s senior data scientist and first-listed author. I found no public evidence of a personal PE payment or network ownership interest tied to this study for either.
How sponsors help shape the work
Tufts says private-sector grants cover roughly 55% of center operating expenses in a typical year and public-sector grants about 45%. The center also receives course and subscription fees. Grant examples include ICON, IQVIA, Parexel and Pfizer. Those are center-wide disclosures. I could not verify the funders or dollar amounts for this study. The ten organizations that contributed data cannot automatically be counted as ten financial sponsors.
Tufts says its faculty and director set the research agenda. Its announcement of this project says working-group companies help shape hypotheses and methods and review and interpret findings. Participants can also receive custom benchmarking reports. That structure gives the center an incentive to produce work its industry partners value. Access to operational data is a real benefit of the arrangement. The disclosure I want is who chose the protocols, who paid, who saw the analysis before publication and who had approval rights. I found no evidence that any author was paid to deliver a favorable result for private equity, but as an independent community-based site owner, I am sure I am speaking for myself and others when I want to make sure that we are being measured on an even playing field when these types of influential "studies" are being distributed to sponsors who have to decide on utilizing more site networks or independent sites. Ultimately every sponsor makes their own call, but in my opinion, this particular study was an unfair representation of independent sites.
Who benefits when the chart reaches a sponsor
Clinical Leader published the Tufts article as a guest column. Its parent, Life Science Connect, received an investment from Latticework Capital Management and Edgehill Management. Latticework describes the publisher as a marketing and lead-generation business. It also formed American Clinical Research Services, which acquired multisite operator Elixia. One investor backed both the publisher and a company competing for clinical trial work. I found no public evidence that Latticework commissioned, edited or paid for the Tufts article.
AMRC’s incentive is more direct. Its membership is open to corporations that wholly own at least five sites. Sponsors directing more work to those companies serves its members. NMS Capital says member Flourish Research made eleven acquisitions and grew revenue more than tenfold before NMS sold it to Genstar. AMRC’s FY2025 tax-return summary records $406,251 in contributions and grants, without identifying the individual payers. Clinical Leader distributed an earlier AMRC survey, and its chief editor also moderated an AMRC panel that included a skeptical independent operator. Tufts and AMRC are listed as collaborators on a separate sponsor-performance project. These are documented business relationships. They leave the funding of the October study open.
Tufts never breaks out completion rates by private equity ownership. The authors call the small sponsor sample their biggest limitation and warn that investor pressure could affect patient engagement. AMRC goes further and gives network affiliation itself credit for the gap.
I’ll give the PE-backed networks credit where I’ve seen them earn it. If I’m a sponsor trying to open five sites, I see the appeal of negotiating one contract and having a dedicated regulatory team get all five moving. That competition has pushed those of us running independent sites to get faster, too. At Yuma, we can show a sponsor how long it takes us to open a study, enter a visit and answer a data query. I think networks have helped raise that standard.
Where I part company with AMRC is patient completion. If a PE-backed network pays a premium for an independent site, part of what it may be buying is a coordinator who already knows the patients and has spent years getting them back for follow-up. That team’s track record is one reason the site is worth buying. I’d like to see what patients at that same site did on comparable trials before and after the acquisition. Then we could start to see how much the network added to what it bought.
If I’m asking Tufts to show its work, I think we ought to show ours. I’d like our SOS Save Our Sites community to partner with sponsors willing to compare dedicated independent sites and network sites on the same trials. Pick the measures up front. How long did it take each site to open? Of the patients each site randomized, how many completed the study, and how many provided the primary endpoint? Collect both measures using definitions agreed up front, along with the reasons patients did not complete. Maybe survey some monitors. Then publish what we find, whichever way it goes.
I know sites like mine do better than that 42% headline suggests. I’ve got 22 years of experience behind that opinion. What I’d like to put behind it now is data a sponsor can use the next time it has to choose a site, but at the very least, provide some healthy skepticism to the industry for scrutinizing the headlines, following the money, and looking at the details because as Darrell Huff warned us more than half a century ago, it is very easy to "Lie With Statistics".  I guess for myself as well as us small site owners, we gotta get used to continuing to punch above our weight class this next decade.

Tencent's latest model isn't a bigger flagship. It's a much cheaper option for everyday AI work. And that price difference is what makes this launch interesting.

Hy4 Flash, released on Monday, has 224 billion parameters but activates just 12 billion per token. It's natively multimodal, supports a million tokens of context, and decodes at more than 150 tokens per second, according to Tencent.

The pricing is what really stands out:

• $0.070 per million input tokens
• $0.281 per million output tokens
• $0.003 per million cached input tokens

Compared with Tencent's flagship Hy4, that's roughly 12 times cheaper on input and 9 times cheaper on output, while the context window stays the same.

Tencent's bigger claim is that Flash can handle everyday office work — documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and research — at one-twentieth of Hy4's cost per task.

But there's a catch.

That figure comes from WorkIndex, Tencent's own internal benchmark built around typical tasks in its own office product. It's not public, so it can't be checked independently.

The other quality claim is based on blind tests involving Tencent's own employees, who reportedly rated Flash's satisfaction close to Claude Haiku 5.5.

Neither result has been independently verified.

So I'd separate this launch into two parts.

The price is real and publicly listed. Anyone can check the rate card and calculate what using the model would cost.

The quality claim is still a promise based on Tencent's own testing.

And that distinction matters because these two claims will be tested at very different speeds. The price can be believed right away. The quality will take months of real workloads to prove.

Here's why I think the pricing matters more than another benchmark score.

AI agents make a lot of model calls. A person might ask a flagship model one difficult question. An agent workflow, on the other hand, might ask a cheaper model thousands of times — checking, drafting, rechecking, and monitoring in the background.

At flagship prices, many of those workflows simply aren't economical.

Cut the cost per task to one-twentieth, and the equation changes. Things that previously weren't worth automating suddenly become worth building, because work that used to happen once, when someone got around to it, can now run continuously.

That's the market Tencent is targeting. Not just better benchmark scores, but a lower cost for every task, because that cost decides which agent workflows are even possible.

There are two caveats worth keeping in mind.

First, the current prices include promotional discounts. Flash is free inside Tencent's WorkBuddy until November 30, and half price on its cloud platform. So part of today's price gap is a sale, not a permanent change.

Second, the open-source release hasn't happened yet. Tencent says it plans to release the weights, but there's no date. The hosted model is available today. The downloadable version is still just a line in a press release.

Hy4 got the attention when it launched two weeks ago. But Flash could end up being the model people actually use, millions of times a day, if the quality holds up.

That's the real test. The price has already changed what developers can afford to build. Now the model has to prove it can deliver.

#AI #OpenSource

The China report is being read as an export-control story. It's also a pricing story. The most valuable thing in a non-exclusive RL environment is the first lab's decision to buy it, and the market pays for that decision with a discount fixed before anyone knows how far the copies will travel.
Here's the line from this year's reporting that I can't stop thinking about. One executive who has spoken to Chinese AI labs told Forbes in August that the labs "explicitly tell U.S. data labelers that they want to buy all the data that the U.S. labs have already purchased."
Read that again. They aren't asking for coding data, or finance rubrics, or a Slack clone. They're asking for whatever the US labs already bought. That's not a data request. That's a request for somebody else's judgment.
On Nov 11, ChinaTalk's Aqib Zakaria and Quinn Ennis published "Piggybacking to the Frontier," naming nine US vendors reported to sell training data, including RL environments, to Chinese labs, in a data trade ChinaTalk puts at roughly half a billion dollars (a figure that traces to Forbes's August reporting and covers all data, not just RL). SemiAnalysis summed up the reaction on X: "Chips are under scrutiny. Data sales to China aren't, yet."
For dual-use domains like cyber and bio, that concern is real, and ChinaTalk treats it carefully. But for most of this trade, I think the framing misses the economics. The leak isn't just a policy gap. It's the business model of non-exclusive data, working as designed. And the most valuable thing being resold isn't the environment. It's the signal that the environment works.
What's actually in the box
Epoch AI interviewed 18 people across RL environment startups, neo-labs and frontier labs. Their interviewees put typical task costs at $200 to $2,000. Mechanize, in an August 2025 back-of-envelope, projected that a frontier RL task would soon burn about $480 of compute per training run, or roughly $2,400 over five reuses. One lab researcher told Epoch that "what everyone does is vibe code a buggy website which isn't useful. There's a large amount of useless bad environments out there."
 
Mechanize's point, which I think is right, is that "data and compute are complementary." If a task's lifetime compute can rival or exceed its price, the expensive mistake isn't overpaying for data. It's training on the wrong data. And rollouts are where most of the training time goes: a paper on RL training from researchers at UIUC, Together AI and others reports the rollout phase "accounts for more than 70% of the total training time."
So the scarcest input in this market isn't the task. It's the knowledge of which tasks are worth the rollouts. ChinaTalk says that is exactly what Chinese labs are buying: they "have been reported to purchase exactly the same products as American labs like Anthropic and OpenAI so as to acquire what they know to be good data."
That's why I call it order flow. In trading, the valuable part of an informed order isn't the hundred shares. It's what the order reveals. Here, a frontier lab's purchase order tells a vendor which domain is next, what spec works, which rubric survived reward hacking, and what difficulty band moved the model. Forbes put it well: "The true secret sauce sits inside the data specifications."
Two caveats. The signal is noisier than a trade print: vendors don't publish who bought what, and an environment calibrated to one model won't transfer one-for-one. And ChinaTalk's sources say Chinese purchasing is "nearly entirely predicated on benchmaxxing," so much of what those labs buy may be a benchmark bump, not a roadmap. Both shrink the effect. Neither zeroes it: Forbes reports off-the-shelf sets are built with the same "knowledge pipelines" developed in custom work for OpenAI or Anthropic.
The first buyer pays to discover what works. Later buyers pay for a copy of the answer.
Vendors already know what they're selling
Look at how off-the-shelf data is marketed now.
Surge AI's off-the-shelf page sells "Training data, evals, and RL environments built by the same experts behind our frontier-lab work," headlines "Proven gains on public benchmarks," and offers Trusted Program partners a deal to "train first, and pay if it works."
 
"Pay if it works" is the tell. The vendor is underwriting the one risk that matters, whether the data actually moves the model. It can offer that because the proof is produced before the sale: the headline results are public models (Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 Super and Moonshot's Kimi K2.7) scored on public benchmarks after training on Surge datasets. That's the vendor retiring the risk up front.
Forbes reports these off-the-shelf datasets "carry the highest profit margins" because they can be resold, and quotes data consultant Sean Cai: "It is extremely easy for a data vendor that has served Anthropic to use the same stack to produce data for a Chinese lab." ChinaTalk adds that after the first sale, "the overhead on selling to other customers is functionally zero," and that because value decays as capabilities diffuse, vendors are "incentivized to dump a product to as many customers as soon as possible."
Zero marginal cost, a perishable product, and a buyer pool that wants whatever the leader bought. That's not a loophole. That's a resale business with a clock on it.
The market already prices the leak: 4x to 5x
Here's the number that does most of the work. Two RL environment founders independently told Epoch that exclusive deals run roughly 4 to 5 times the price of non-exclusive ones. ChinaTalk uses the same figure: American labs "may pay up to four or five times more for an exclusive product to avoid this piggybacking." Hannah Xu heard the same range this month: exclusive deals "run 4-5x non-exclusive ones."
Think about what that premium is. If a vendor prices exclusivity at break-even, it should be indifferent between one exclusive sale and N non-exclusive sales when N roughly equals the premium. On that reading, 4x to 5x implies the vendor expects about four or five paying copies before the product goes stale. It's a rough read: the premium also prices confidentiality for the buyer, custom work bundled into exclusives, cash now versus uncertain resale, and later copies that sell for less.
It also means the first lab isn't giving its decision away. A lab that buys non-exclusive pays roughly a quarter to a fifth of the exclusive price, and that discount is its payment for letting the vendor resell. The real question is whether a discount fixed at signing is the right price for a signal whose value depends on how far, and how fast, the copies travel.
 
Now ask who those buyers are. Forbes reports the top six Chinese labs spend about $500 million a year with American data companies, per two entrepreneurs who received estimates from Tencent and ByteDance executives, and, per one person who has dealt with several of them, that those labs see themselves "as a collective buyer pool looking for top-tier Western datasets."
This is where I part ways with the consensus take. If some of those expected copies go to Chinese labs, then Chinese demand is part of what makes the non-exclusive price cheap for everyone else, including US labs. Strip that pool out by rule and you don't make data safer for free. You shrink N, and vendors either charge the remaining buyers more for a copy or spend less building it.
That's my inference, not a reported fact. But it means "ban the sales" is not a free lunch for American labs. It's a price change. The labs already have private versions of that control: exclusives, custom builds and in-house teams. How often they pay for them rather than take the discount is one of the least-disclosed numbers in this market.
 
What export rules can and can't do
I'm not against ChinaTalk's proposals. For dual-use domains they're the right tool: BIS restricting dual-use environments under existing rules, is-informed letters to vendors, and procurement rules for defense contractors are narrow and sensible, and the authors themselves argue the trade isn't apocalyptic: piggybacking needs a US lab to buy first, which keeps the buyer "at least a few months behind."
But read their own reporting on enforcement. Work runs under client codenames, so contractors "often don't know the end buyer." RL environments are largely outside export controls except for Entity-Listed buyers, and ChinaTalk says Mercor narrowed its customer policy in May 2026 from an ownership test to a location test. Even exclusivity leaks: "tacit knowledge trickles down," because a vendor that can't resell the exact clone can still skip its own mistakes on the next one.
Letters can move fast. Broad rules can't, and this product loses value on a model-release calendar. Rules can fence off dual-use domains. They can't price the rest of the market.
For everything else, the layer that moves at the speed of the market is the contract, and there are two contracts in every environment: the one between vendor and lab, and the one under the data itself.
The contract nobody's reading
ChinaTalk drops a line near the end that deserves its own article. Environments "built on proprietary data — i.e., data that is the property of an American lab — cannot be resold." And then: "We should be curious about the extent to which contracts brokering data between vendors and businesses, particularly SMEs, are being heeded."
The same report notes that for coding environments, vendors spend "huge amounts of money purchasing company GitHub repos," bugs and fixes included. So a lot of this order flow sits on top of some company's real operating history.
This is the part I see from the supply side. At Heartland we license established companies' operational  on time-limited terms. From that seat, the source-data license is the one point in this chain where resale is a breach by default, not a clause someone has to pay 4x to 5x for. Who the licensee is, how long the term runs, whether sublicensing is allowed: those three clauses decide whether a dataset can ever become somebody else's off-the-shelf SKU. A time limit also matches how this product actually behaves. It's perishable. Perpetual rights to perishable goods mostly benefit whoever resells them last.
Hannah Xu, who has been catching up with labs and data vendors lately, wrote last week that "labs now pay most for data on what their models get wrong," and that "Volume got cheap." I agree, and I'd add one thing: data aimed at a weak spot is only worth a premium while the weak spot is private. Once the purchase order is shared, so is the weakness.
What I expect next
Three things, all falsifiable.
Exclusivity gets priced by the month. Exclusive windows and first-look rights already exist. I expect them to get shorter, cheaper and more explicit, with release to the resale market written in, because the product decays. The first buyer pays for being first, not for owning a melting ice cube.
More in-housing at the frontier. One founder told Epoch in January there's been "substantially more in-housing," and Epoch lists keeping training priorities confidential among the reasons. ChinaTalk notes sensitive domains are moving inside the labs. That's the frontier opting out of the order-flow market.
Off-the-shelf becomes the fast-follower market, openly. "Proven gains" and "pay if it works" pricing is a product for buyers who want the second copy. That market will be big, it will be global, and it will be priced on proof, some produced by the vendor and some inherited from the first buyer.
How much any of this matters depends on a debate that played out between Dwarkesh Patel and Amjad Masad this weekend. Patel argued gains are "mostly the general learning algorithm getting better." Masad asked how much comes from "domain-specific data and RL environments," given "the magnitude of investment in the latter." If Patel is right, piggybacking matters less. If Masad is right, the most valuable thing a frontier lab produces besides weights is its shopping list, and every non-exclusive purchase puts part of that list on the market at a discount.
Data is cheap to copy. Decisions are expensive to make. Right now the market prices the second with a discount set at signing. That's the part I expect to change.

GPT-6.1 Terra took over slide repair on Oct 29. It cut the share of slides still failing after repair from 9.1% to 4.7%.

Anthropic still holds the hardest job. Claude Sonnet 5.5 plans the deck with the user, and Gamma says those plans were rated good about 18% more often.

Gamma also trained its own repair model. It fixed 76% of failing slides on the first try, against 57% for the general model it was tested against.

My read: OpenAI had 11.5% of Gamma's spend in the week ending Sep 7 and 43.7% by Nov 6. That's about 3.8x in two months, in a business that tests every new model on real users.
